AG2 outperforms fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1 and specialized models trained on target datasets, doubling recall of causal single-cell eQTLs at 90% precision. AG2 also achieves state-of-the-art enhancer-gene linking and can pinpoint causal variants at complex trait loci. Across hundreds of human cell types, we generated an atlas of enhancer-gene links and scores for 7 million common variants. As single-cell profiling expands across development, tissues, and disease cohorts, AG2 provides a blueprint for turning observational atlases into variant effect maps.

title: GausSKAT: A Data-Adaptive Weighted Gaussian Kernel Procedure for Rare-Variant Association Testing Within the SKAT Framework
summary: SKAT almost always uses a weighted-linear kernel, and how well a Gaussian kernel works depends on a bandwidth that cannot be chosen in advance. GausSKAT runs weighted Gaussian SKAT over a data-driven, phenotype-independent grid of bandwidths and combines the resulting p-values with ACAT. In simulations it generally had more power than weighted-linear and IBS SKAT; in Dallas Heart Study triglyceride data its advantage over linear SKAT varied across ANGPTL gene sets.
abstract: Genome-wide association studies have limited power to detect rare-variant associations. The sequence kernel association test (SKAT) enhances power by jointly testing variants within a region, but its power depends on how the kernel represents genetic similarity. The weighted-linear kernel predominates in rare-variant testing, whereas the weighted Gaussian kernel remains less widely used. Varying the Gaussian bandwidth hyperparameter changes the representation of genetic similarity from localized and nonlinear to increasingly linear-like. However, very small hyperparameter values can cause similarities between nonidentical weighted genotype profiles to collapse toward zero, whereas very large values cause the weighted Gaussian kernel to behave increasingly like weighted-linear SKAT and therefore provide little distinct information. Because the underlying genetic architecture is unknown, no single hyperparameter value can be expected to work best across regions. We propose GausSKAT, which evaluates weighted Gaussian SKAT over a phenotype-independent, data-adaptive hyperparameter grid and combines the resulting dependent p values using the aggregated Cauchy association test (ACAT). The grid endpoints are informed by weighted genetic distances and the large-hyperparameter behavior of the covariate-adjusted kernel. In simulations, GausSKAT generally achieved higher power than weighted-linear and weighted identity-by-state SKAT under the genetic architectures considered. The best-performing hyperparameter value varied across settings, supporting aggregation across multiple values. In the Dallas Heart Study analysis of triglyceride levels, the relative performance of GausSKAT and weighted-linear SKAT varied among ANGPTL gene-family variant sets. These findings support GausSKAT as a complementary extension that broadens the similarity structures represented within SKAT.

title: Polygenic risk scores for sleep: from portability to clinical utility
summary: Single-author perspective on polygenic risk scores for sleep traits and disorders, covering how well they transfer across populations and whether they are clinically useful. No abstract is available, so this summary is based on the title only.

title: Population-Scale, Genotype-First Characterization of Monogenic Diabetes in 374,973 Individuals Across Ancestries in the NIH All of Us Research Program
summary: Using WGS from 374,973 All of Us participants (42% non-European), the authors found pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 10 MODY genes in about 1 in 1,013 people, at similar rates in European and African ancestry groups. Diabetes penetrance was incomplete (43.5% by age 60) and was highest for GCK and lowest for non-GCK/HNF genes, whose carrier risk was below that of non-carriers in the top type 2 diabetes PRS decile. Higher T2D polygenic risk further raised diabetes risk among carriers.
abstract: Current understanding of maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) has been shaped by phenotype-first studies in predominantly European ancestry cohorts, leaving population-level prevalence and penetrance in a multiancestry population incompletely defined. Using a genotype-first design, we analyzed whole-genome sequencing and clinical data from 374,973 unrelated All of Us participants (42.0% non-European ancestry). We identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 10 established MODY genes and assessed carrier prevalence, diabetes penetrance, and age-dependent diabetes risk, including comparisons with noncarriers stratified by type 2 diabetes polygenic risk score (T2D PRS) and associations between T2D PRS and diabetes risk among carriers. We identified 370 carriers (0.099%; 1 in 1,013), with similar prevalence among European and African ancestry participants (0.105% in both). Diabetes penetrance was incomplete (13.4% by age 40; 43.5% by age 60) and varied by etiology: highest for GCK (56.0% by age 60), intermediate for HNF genes (HNF1A, HNF1B, and HNF4A; 45.4%), and lowest for non-GCK/HNF genes (ABCC8, INS, KCNJ11, NEUROD1, PDX1, and RFX6; 29.0%). In Cox models, carriers of variants in non-GCK/HNF genes had modestly increased diabetes risk (hazard ratio [HR] 1.64; 95% CI 1.19-2.27), which was numerically lower than among noncarriers in the top 10% of T2D PRS (HR 1.91; 95% CI 1.87-1.95). Higher T2D PRS was also associated with greater diabetes risk among carriers (HR per SD 1.32; 95% CI 1.13-1.56). These findings support equitable consideration of MODY genetic testing across ancestries and highlight substantial heterogeneity in diabetes risk among carriers of pathogenic variants in MODY genes.
